newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA RAND, RESERVES TO WEATHER FX EASING -POLL.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA RAND, RESERVES TO WEATHER FX EASING -POLL.

text.p: South Africa's rand is set to depreciate gradually, cushioned by improved official reserves which will remain at comfortable levels despite the easing of exchange controls on July 1, a Reuters poll showed on Thursday.
The currency is likely to reach 4.68 against the U.S. dollar by the end of 1997 and 4.97 by end 1998, according to the consensus forecast of 31 economists.
The spot rand was last trading around 4.51, six month forward rates were at around 4.72 and 12-month forward rates at about 4.91 against the dollar.
Reserves of gold and foreign exchange held by the central bank were expected to remain around current record levels, despite the move to allow individuals to invest offshore from next month.

Official reserves were predicted to stand at 22.1 billion rand by the end of August, two months on from the relaxation of exchange controls which will allow individuals to invest up to 200,000 rand ($44,400) overseas.
Gross gold and foreign exchange reserves stood at 21.8 billion rand at May 31.

In addition, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Wednesday the central bank had access to a further 16 billion rand which could be used to supply liquidity to the market in the event of significant capital flight.
His deputy, James Cross, estimated that between three and five billion rand could leave the country post July 1, but that this would be matched by inflows -- a sentiment echoed by economists.
"We are a very highly-indebted, low-savings-base economy, so I really can't see a dramatic run for the door come next week," said Investec Bank economist Carole Mason.
"By and large the possible outflows will be neutralised by the amount of money coming in, and there might be small net gain," she added.
SocGen Frankel Pollak economist Mike Brown said he expected around five billion rand to leave the country and that the removal of controls on individuals was likely to be a non-event.
"We may have a small depreciation of the currency which would be in our favour," Brown said.
"I think the rand is a little bit overvalued at the moment...it would do no harm at all to the South African economy to have a marginal decline in the currency," he said.
